name: Nitrogen-fixing wheat
subtitle: wheat that makes its own fertiliser

effects.effect: a guided enzyme cuts DNA at any spot spelled out by a short RNA
plants need nitrogen from the soil
a cell can run on a genome written entirely by computer

effect: a guided enzyme cuts DNA at any spot spelled out by a short RNA
how: Making nitrogen fertiliser consumes a couple of percent of the world's energy, and most of what is spread runs off into rivers; beans avoid all of it by housing bacteria in root nodules, and cereals cannot. Cereals still carry most of the genes for the conversation a root has with those bacteria, so a guided enzyme can wake and rewire that pathway, while the partner bacterium gets a written genome tuned to the new host, until wheat roots build nodules of their own.
obstacle: Nodules cost a plant sugar it would otherwise put into grain, and despite decades of work no cereal has yet made one.
why: Would retire the single largest industrial energy use in agriculture.
real: Decades of attempts to give cereals functional root nodules have failed; the closest working result is UC Davis CRISPR wheat that exudes extra apigenin to stimulate free-living soil bacteria to fix nitrogen (greenhouse yield gain, Plant Biotech J 2025) - the same job by a different, nodule-free mechanism.
